title: Married and single (1 Corinthians 7)
hookLine: Paul answers their questions practically, honoring both marriage and singleness
tomorrow: you're right about the facts. is that the end of it?

cards: An advice column. An anonymous question box. A group chat full of 'asking for a friend.' Paul gets the old version: "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me".

The Corinthians have mailed him their questions, and the first ones are about marriage, sex and staying single. Chapter seven reads like half a phone call: we hear Paul's answers and have to guess the questions.

teach.b: Today's question: is a single life a lesser life? Paul answers personally: "For I would that all men were even as I myself." He seems to be unmarried, and content.
But he won't make it a rule: "But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." Marriage is a gift. Singleness is a gift.

Neither is the backup plan. And he's careful about whose voice is speaking: on divorce, "I command, yet not I, but the Lord"; on another question, "I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment".
A neighbor tradition keeps two honored ways of life too.
In Buddhism, monks and nuns leave home for the path, and the Buddha also taught householders.
In the Sigalovada Sutta he tells a young man how a husband honors his wife, with respect, courtesy and faithfulness, and how she cares for him and the household in return.
That's shared ground: a vowed single life and a married life, each with its place. The honest difference is the reason.
For Paul, singleness frees undivided attention for the Lord, and both ways are a gift of God.
The Buddhist monk or nun leaves home to let go of craving on the way to nirvana.

how: Christians read 1 Corinthians 7 in different ways: Catholic and Orthodox churches draw on it in honoring vowed single life, and other churches turn to it in teaching on marriage and singleness.

games.why: Paul wishes all were as he is, then refuses to make it a rule: every man hath his proper gift of God.

practice: Bring to mind three people whose lives look different from yours: married, single, widowed, still waiting. For each, count one honest gift you see in their life, without measuring it against your own.
Let each gift stay as it is, theirs and good.
